projects.name: Hybrid VQC Weather Forecasting with FPGA Inference
projects.blurb: 7-qubit variational circuit for 24-day temperature forecasting, with a custom kernel on an AMD Alveo FPGA for low-latency edge inference.
projects.abstract: A hybrid quantum-classical model that forecasts temperature 24 days ahead from daily NCMRWF reanalysis data, using a 7-qubit variational quantum circuit (50 parameters) with StronglyEntanglingLayers. For low-latency inference, the frozen model runs on a custom AMD Alveo U55C FPGA kernel built with HLS.
projects.role: Lead developer — algorithm design, training pipeline, and FPGA deployment.

sections.p: Medium-range (24-day-ahead) temperature forecasting is hard: atmospheric dynamics are nonlinear and labelled data is limited. The question was whether a compact variational quantum circuit, trained on daily NCMRWF reanalysis data, could learn useful long-range patterns, and whether its inference could run fast enough for edge use.

I designed a 7-qubit variational quantum circuit with 50 trainable parameters, using angle encoding to map meteorological variables onto the qubits and two StronglyEntanglingLayers as the ansatz. It was trained, validated and tested in PennyLane on a CPU-based quantum simulator, reaching a test RMSE of 3.01 K and R² of 0.801.

For low-latency edge inference, the frozen model runs on a custom Vitis HLS kernel on an AMD Alveo U55C FPGA; the kernel exchanges batches of input features, pre-trained weights and expectation values with the host over HBM.
A hybrid VQC forecaster with low-latency FPGA inference for edge use. Published at IEEE TQCEBT 2026.

projects.name: Quantum Image Representation Neural Networks
projects.blurb: Quantum neural networks for binary image classification built on four quantum image encodings: NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI.
projects.abstract: Quantum neural networks that classify binary MNIST images (0 vs 1) at 2×2, 4×4 and 8×8, with pixel data encoded through four quantum image representations: NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI. It compares circuit depth, gate count and qubit usage for the four encodings; QBIR gives the shallowest circuits, FRQCI the deepest. Published in The Journal of Supercomputing 82:495 (2026).

sections.p: Quantum image classification depends heavily on how classical pixel data is encoded into quantum states, but encodings are often chosen by convention rather than by measured trade-off.

I built quantum neural networks on four quantum image representations — NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI — for binary MNIST classification (0 vs 1) at 2×2, 4×4 and 8×8. It compares circuit depth, gate count and qubit usage for the four encodings; QBIR gives the shallowest circuits, FRQCI the deepest.
Published in The Journal of Supercomputing 82:495 (2026).

projects.name: Linear-Optical QKD Network Testbeds
projects.blurb: DPS, COW, and Twin-Field QKD simulated over realistic photonic channels with security analysis.
projects.abstract: Simulation testbeds for differential-phase-shift (DPS), coherent-one-way (COW), and Twin-Field QKD protocols over lossy, noisy photonic channels. Includes security analysis against intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks, plus Python tooling for optical simulation post-processing.
projects.role: Research fellow — simulation design, security analysis, and tooling.

sections.p: QKD protocols are usually analysed under idealised channel assumptions. Deployment behaviour depends on loss, detector noise, and attacker models that idealised analysis omits.

I built simulation testbeds for three protocols — differential-phase-shift (DPS), coherent-one-way (COW), and Twin-Field QKD — in OptiSystem and ANSYS, modelling realistic photonic loss and noise across the channel.

Each protocol was evaluated against intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks, with key-rate degradation quantified as a function of channel loss. I also benchmarked resource-state and entanglement generation.
Optical simulators produce large, awkward output. I wrote Python post-processing tooling to make the analysis reusable and maintainable rather than a manual per-run effort.

projects.name: Quantum Circuits for Block Ciphers
projects.blurb: Mini-AES / S-AES circuits with a Grover-based plaintext–ciphertext attack demonstration.
projects.abstract: Quantum circuit designs for Mini-AES and S-AES block ciphers with Galois-field arithmetic, validated on Qiskit simulators and IBM Quantum hardware. Demonstrates a plaintext–ciphertext attack via Grover's search and amplitude amplification.
projects.role: Research intern — circuit design and attack demonstration.

sections.p: Understanding how symmetric ciphers degrade under quantum attack requires explicit, runnable circuit constructions, not just asymptotic arguments.
I designed quantum circuits for Mini-AES and S-AES, including the Galois-field arithmetic that the S-box depends on, and validated them on Qiskit simulators and IBM Quantum hardware.
I demonstrated a plaintext–ciphertext attack using Grover's search with amplitude amplification, making the quadratic speedup concrete on a scaled-down cipher.
Work also covered circuit optimisation and error-correction considerations for running these constructions on noisy devices.

projects.name: Entanglement Detection via Neural Networks (NMR)
projects.blurb: An ANN that detects genuine multipartite entanglement and assigns SLOCC classes on a three-qubit NMR processor from 18 of 128 density-matrix elements.
projects.abstract: An artificial neural network that detects genuine multipartite entanglement and assigns one of six SLOCC classes to three-qubit states, using 18 of the 128 density-matrix elements, ranked by ANOVA. Validated on 30 experimental states from an NMR quantum processor. Published in Quantum Information Processing 24(3), 74 (2025).
projects.role: Co-first author (equal contribution with V. Gulati); MS research student.

sections.p: Detecting genuine multipartite entanglement in experimental NMR systems is hard: witnesses are state-specific and full state tomography is experimentally costly.

I designed an ANN that detects genuine multipartite entanglement and assigns one of six SLOCC classes from a reduced set of density-matrix elements: states in canonical form, 128 elements reduced to 18, then ranked by ANOVA.
Validated on 30 experimental three-qubit states from an NMR processor, GME detection remained accurate with 4 features and SLOCC classification with 6.
Published in Quantum Information Processing 24(3), 74 (2025); preprint arXiv:2409.19739.

projects.name: VQLS for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
projects.blurb: A variational quantum linear solver applied end to end to next-day stock price forecasting on real market data.
projects.abstract: A variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) applied to time series forecasting on real financial market data. Hankel-like trajectory matrices are built from historical Reliance Industries stock prices and the resulting linear system is solved with a quantum-classical hybrid approach: Hadamard test circuits evaluate the cost function, COBYLA optimizes the variational parameters, and a SWAP test extracts the solution to produce next-day price forecasts. Quantum advantage is not realized at this problem scale (2 × 2 system), and classical baselines reach equivalent accuracy; the work establishes a verified pathway for VQLS deployment on NISQ devices and identifies its scalability bottlenecks.

sections.p: Existing VQLS demonstrations focus on synthetic test cases; practical deployment on domain-specific data remains sparse. The question was whether the quantum-classical hybrid architecture can be validated on an authentic forecasting workflow before hardware scales.

A Hankel-like trajectory matrix is built from daily closing prices of Reliance Industries (January to April 2023) and decomposed into a Pauli basis. Hadamard test circuits evaluate the VQLS cost function, COBYLA optimizes the variational parameter with 10,000 shots per circuit, and a SWAP test combines the solution with recent market data to give a next-day forecast. All circuits run in Qiskit on the Aer simulator.

The workflow runs end to end and the solution is verified against AR(1) and linear regression baselines. Quantum advantage is not realized at this 2 × 2 scale, and the classical baselines reach equivalent accuracy in negligible time. The paper identifies the scalability bottlenecks: exponential growth of the Pauli decomposition and COBYLA shot overhead.
Published by IEEE, 2026.

projects.name: TensNet: Tensor Networks for 2D Flow Simulation
projects.blurb: A tensor network library using MPS and MPO for memory-efficient simulation of 2D incompressible flow.
projects.abstract: TensNet is a library implementing tensor network methods, using Matrix Product States (MPS) and Matrix Product Operators (MPO), for memory-efficient simulation of the 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. It keeps solution accuracy through adaptive bond-dimension truncation, uses the DMRG algorithm to solve the implicit pressure-correction equations, and uses cross-approximation to handle complex immersed boundaries, reducing the memory footprint relative to traditional methods.

sections.p: Computational fluid dynamics simulations demand enormous memory for storing high-resolution velocity fields, which is a barrier to practical simulations on resource-constrained systems.

TensNet represents flow fields as Matrix Product States and operators as Matrix Product Operators, compressing them by SVD truncation with adaptive bond dimensions. The two-site DMRG algorithm solves the implicit Poisson equations in the pressure-correction scheme, and cross-approximation represents immersed boundaries and obstacle geometries as MPS.
Benchmarks include a cylinder in cross-flow and arrays of circular obstacles, with drag coefficients and Strouhal numbers compared against reference values.
Manuscript in preparation.

about.headline: Bridging quantum theory and shipped software.
statement: My work sits at the seam between quantum information research and production engineering. I am interested in the question of what it actually takes to move a quantum algorithm off a whiteboard and onto hardware that runs under real constraints — noise, latency, memory bandwidth, and the unglamorous requirement that it keep working next week.

That has led me across three connected areas. In variational quantum algorithms and quantum machine learning, I study how circuit structure and data encoding govern trainability and expressivity, and how hybrid pipelines perform on real forecasting tasks. In quantum hardware acceleration, I compile trained quantum kernels down to FPGA fabric for low-latency inference, which is a systems-engineering problem as much as a quantum one. In photonic quantum networks, I simulate QKD protocols over lossy channels and analyse their security against realistic attacks.

What connects them is a conviction that quantum computing progresses fastest when research artefacts are built like software — tested, versioned, reproducible, and deployable. I want to keep working where those two cultures meet.
